question: Inertia
content: Newton's First Law states that an object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion along a straight line, unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force.
description: Your company has used the same payroll software for twelve years. Everyone complains about it, but nobody has switched. What physical principle explains this stagnation?
options: Entropy — systems naturally degrade over time
Friction — the software is difficult to learn
Inertia of rest — the organization is at rest and requires
Activation energy — the cost of change is perceived as too high
answer: Inertia of rest — the organization is at rest and requires
explanation: The organization has 'social mass.' Even though people complain, the system is at rest relative to change. Overcoming this inertia requires a concentrated, disproportionate burst of energy to break the static equilibrium.

question: Inertia of Motion
content: Once an object with significant mass is in motion, it tends to stay in motion, barreling past obstacles due to its momentum.
description: A dominant social media platform continues growing despite multiple privacy scandals, regulatory fines, and public backlash. Users keep joining. What best explains this?
options: Users do not care about privacy
The company has excellent public relations
Network effects and user base mass create
Regulatory fines are too small to matter
answer: Network effects and user base mass create
explanation: Once a platform reaches critical mass, its own momentum carries it forward. New users join because existing users are there. This inertia of motion makes it extremely difficult to halt or redirect, regardless of external shocks.

question: Social Mass
content: The resistance to change in an organization is proportional to its 'social mass' — the size, tenure, cultural entrenchment, and complexity of the system.
description: A 50-person startup pivots its product in three weeks. A 50,000-person enterprise tries the same pivot and fails after nine months. What explains the difference?
options: Enterprise employees are less capable than startup employees
Startups have fewer legal restrictions on product changes
The enterprise has higher social mass — more people, processes,
The enterprise lacked the financial resources to execute the pivot
answer: The enterprise has higher social mass — more people, processes,
explanation: Inertia is proportional to mass. A startup's low social mass allows rapid direction changes. A large enterprise's high social mass — accumulated through years of processes, headcount, culture, and legacy tech — resists any change in trajectory.

question: Overcoming the At-Rest Phase
content: When trying to launch a new initiative, you must apply sustained, concentrated force to overcome the initial static friction. A single memo or meeting will not suffice.
description: A newly hired Chief Innovation Officer wants to launch a company-wide AI upskilling program. After one kickoff presentation, participation is negligible. What did they underestimate?
options: Employees are lazy and will avoid any optional program
The program was not mandated from the top, so nobody feels obligated to attend
Overcoming the organization's inertia of rest requires sustained, repeated
AI skills are not relevant to most employees' roles
answer: Overcoming the organization's inertia of rest requires sustained, repeated
explanation: Organizational inertia of rest cannot be broken by a single event. It requires a campaign: repeated messaging, executive sponsorship, small pilot groups, incentives, and removal of barriers. Only sustained, concentrated force overcomes the initial static friction.

question: Momentum Investing
content: In financial markets, assets that have already demonstrated strong price momentum tend to continue in that direction, as institutional inertia and herding behavior reinforce the trend.
description: A value investor refuses to buy a stock that has already doubled, believing it is 'too late.' The stock doubles again in the next year. What mental model could have predicted this continued rise?
options: Mean reversion — what goes up must come down
once an asset gains momentum, it tends to continue until acted upon by
The efficient market hypothesis — all information is already priced in
Loss aversion — investors are afraid of buying at the top
answer: once an asset gains momentum, it tends to continue until acted upon by
explanation: Momentum is a real force in markets. Once a trend is established — driven by capital inflows, analyst coverage, and investor enthusiasm — it takes significant contrary force to stop it. Betting against momentum without a clear catalyst is fighting inertia.

question: Force Magnitude Mismatch
content: Leaders often underestimate the magnitude of force required to change an organization's trajectory, applying small nudges when structural force is needed.
description: A CEO sends a strongly worded email about reducing bureaucracy but sees no change in decision-making speed six months later. What went wrong?
options: The CEO did not follow up with enough emails to reinforce the message
structural changes to hierarchies and incentives are required
Middle managers actively sabotaged the CEO's directive
Bureaucracy is an unavoidable feature of any large organization
answer: structural changes to hierarchies and incentives are required
explanation: Inertia is proportional to mass. Entrenched bureaucracy has high social mass accumulated over years. A single email is negligible force. Structural change requires structural force: redesigning systems, realigning incentives, and physically removing friction points.

question: External Force Requirement
content: An object in a state of equilibrium will remain there unless an unbalanced external force acts upon it. Internal dissatisfaction alone does not create motion.
description: A team has been complaining about their legacy workflow for years. A new competitor emerges, stealing 20% of their market share. Within a month, the team adopts a modern workflow. What caused the change?
options: The team finally realized they were inefficient
The competitive threat provided the necessary external force
The new workflow became easier to use over time
Management threatened to fire the team if they did not change
answer: The competitive threat provided the necessary external force
explanation: Internal complaints alone rarely overcome inertia because they do not constitute an unbalanced external force. The competitive threat — an external, existential pressure — provided the concentrated force needed to break the static equilibrium and drive real change.

question: Trajectory Persistence
content: An organization moving in a particular direction will continue on that trajectory unless redirected by a significant force. Minor course corrections rarely alter the overall path.
description: A car manufacturer has been building large SUVs for twenty years. Despite launching a small electric car division, 95% of revenue still comes from large trucks. What principle explains this persistence?
options: The small car division lacks marketing budget
the EV division is too small a force to redirect the
Customers do not want small electric cars from this brand
Electric cars are not profitable for the company
answer: the EV division is too small a force to redirect the
explanation: An organization's trajectory is the vector of its total mass. A small division is a minor force that cannot significantly redirect a large, moving organization. Truly changing direction requires applying force proportional to the entire mass, not just adding a side project.
